# Introduction

Bayesian statistical methods are increasingly used in clinical trial design
and analysis, offering flexible incorporation of prior knowledge and natural
uncertainty quantification [@FDA2026]. However, the widespread adoption of
Bayesian methods in regulatory settings requires that prior distributions be
not only well-chosen but also transparently documented and demonstrably robust.
The FDA's 2026 draft guidance on Bayesian methods [@FDA2026] explicitly
requires sponsors to demonstrate that trial conclusions hold under
sensitivity analyses over the prior specification, yet provides no
methodological framework for how this should be done.

In practice, prior specification often proceeds informally. Analysts may
elicit a prior from clinical literature or expert opinion without a
structured procedure, assess prior-data conflict informally by visual
inspection, and document the justification in narrative form. This approach
is difficult to reproduce and rarely satisfies regulatory reviewers who
expect a systematic, auditable justification.

Existing R packages for Bayesian clinical trials focus on posterior
computation and adaptive design. \CRANpkg{RBesT} [@RBesT] implements
robust meta-analytic-predictive priors for historical data borrowing.
\CRANpkg{trialr} [@trialr] provides a range of adaptive trial designs
via Stan. \CRANpkg{hdbayes} [@hdbayes] implements multiple historical
data borrowing priors -- including power priors, normalised power priors,
robust MAP priors, and commensurate priors -- for generalised linear
models. Each of these tools addresses a specific stage of the Bayesian
workflow well, but none carries a prior through construction from expert
knowledge, prior-data conflict assessment, and regulatory reporting as a
single connected process.

We introduce \CRANpkg{bayprior}, an R package and Shiny application that
connects these stages by providing an integrated prior justification
workflow: structured expert elicitation, expert opinion pooling,
prior-data conflict diagnostics, sensitivity analysis, robust and
regulatory prior alternatives, and automated regulatory reporting. The
package implements established statistical methodology [@OHagan2006;
@Box1980; @Oakley2010; @Schmidli2014; @Ibrahim2000; @Spiegelhalter1994]
in a unified, accessible framework suitable for both programmatic use and
interactive exploration via the bundled Shiny application.

# Related software

## Expert Elicitation

The Sheffield Elicitation Framework [@Oakley2010] provides a structured
approach to expert elicitation and is implemented in the R package
\CRANpkg{SHELF} [@SHELF]. \CRANpkg{SHELF} supports elicitation from
individual or multiple experts across a range of distribution families,
with weighted linear pooling for aggregating multiple expert beliefs.
\CRANpkg{bayprior} extends this with three programmatic elicitation
methods (quantile matching, moment matching, and the roulette method)
across six distribution families, adds logarithmic opinion pooling as
a complement to linear pooling, and introduces quantitative agreement
diagnostics via the Bhattacharyya coefficient for assessing
inter-expert consistency before pooling.

## Robust Priors and Historical Borrowing

\CRANpkg{RBesT} [@RBesT] implements the robust meta-analytic-predictive
(MAP) prior approach [@Schmidli2014] for incorporating historical control
data. \CRANpkg{hdbayes} [@hdbayes] provides a broader range of historical
borrowing methods, including power priors, normalised power priors,
commensurate priors, and robust MAP priors, for generalised linear models
via Stan. \CRANpkg{bayprior} provides the Schmidli robust mixture prior
and calibrated power priors [@Ibrahim2000] as alternatives within the prior
justification workflow, but focuses on prior specification and justification
rather than historical data meta-analysis.

## Prior Sensitivity and Conflict Diagnostics

\CRANpkg{priorsense} [@priorsense] implements power-scaling sensitivity
analysis for detecting prior-data conflict and likelihood noninformativity
in fitted Stan models [@Kallioinen2023]. \CRANpkg{bayprior} addresses a
complementary use case: closed-form conflict diagnostics for conjugate
prior families at the prior specification stage, before any model is
fitted, without requiring Stan. The two packages serve different points
in the Bayesian workflow.

## Scope Comparison

Table 1 summarises the scope of existing packages
relative to \CRANpkg{bayprior}.

```{r pkg-comparison, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(

                    "priorsense", "bayprior"),
    Elicitation = c("Yes",     "No",    "No",     "No",
                    "No",       "Yes"),
    Pooling     = c("Partial", "No",    "No",     "No",
                    "No",       "Yes"),

                    "Yes",      "Yes"),

                        "No",   "Yes"),
    Reporting   = c("No",      "No",    "No",     "No",

```

# Package overview

\CRANpkg{bayprior} is built using the \CRANpkg{golem} [@golem] framework
and provides both exported R functions for programmatic use and a modular
Shiny application for interactive exploration. The package is available on
CRAN and can be installed with:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("bayprior")

# Or the development version from GitHub:
pak::pak("ndohpenngit/bayprior")
```

The Shiny application can be launched with:

```{r run-app, eval=FALSE}
library(bayprior)
run_app()
```

## Prior Elicitation

\CRANpkg{bayprior} implements three structured elicitation approaches
across six distribution families (Beta, Normal, Gamma, Log-Normal,
Exponential, and Weibull).

**Moment matching** derives hyperparameters analytically from an
expert-supplied mean and standard deviation:

```{r elicitation-moments}
prior <- elicit_beta(
  mean      = 0.35,
  sd        = 0.10,
  method    = "moments",
  label     = "Response rate",
  expert_id = "Expert_1"
)
```

```{r prior-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Distribution", "alpha", "beta", "Method", "Expert",
                  "Mean (SD)", "95% CrI"),
    Value = c(
      toupper(prior$dist),
      round(prior$params$alpha, 4),
      round(prior$params$beta, 4),
      paste(prior$method, "elicitation"),
      prior$expert_id,
      paste0(round(prior$fit_summary$mean, 4), " (",
             round(prior$fit_summary$sd, 4), ")"),
      paste0("[", round(prior$fit_summary$q025, 4), ", ",
             round(prior$fit_summary$q975, 4), "]")
    )
  ),
  caption = "Elicited Beta prior for the response rate (moment matching)."
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

**Quantile matching** fits the distribution numerically to expert-specified
probability--value pairs, accommodating asymmetric beliefs that moment
matching cannot capture. For example, an expert who believes the response
rate has a 25\% chance of being below 0.20, a 60\% chance of being below
0.35, and an 80\% chance of being below 0.50:

```{r elicitation-quantile}
prior_qm <- elicit_beta(
  quantiles = c(`0.25` = 0.20, `0.60` = 0.35, `0.80` = 0.50),
  method    = "quantile",
  label     = "Response rate (quantile)",
  expert_id = "Expert_1"
)
```

```{r elicitation-plot, fig.cap="Beta prior elicited by moment matching (mean = 0.35, SD = 0.10). Shaded region shows the 95\\% credible interval."}
plot(prior)
```

The fitted distribution, parameter estimates, and a 95\% credible interval
are displayed automatically. All six families share a common API, so
`elicit_beta()` can be replaced with `elicit_normal()`, `elicit_gamma()`,
`elicit_lognormal()`, `elicit_exponential()`, or `elicit_weibull()` with
identical syntax.

## Expert Pooling

Multiple expert priors can be aggregated using linear or logarithmic
opinion pooling [@OHagan2006]. Linear pooling takes the weighted average
of the densities; logarithmic pooling takes the weighted geometric mean.

```{r pooling}
e1 <- elicit_beta(mean = 0.30, sd = 0.08, method = "moments",
                  label = "Response rate", expert_id = "Expert_1")
e2 <- elicit_beta(mean = 0.42, sd = 0.10, method = "moments",
                  label = "Response rate", expert_id = "Expert_2")

consensus <- aggregate_experts(
  priors  = list(E1 = e1, E2 = e2),
  weights = c(0.5, 0.5),
  method  = "linear"
)
```

```{r consensus-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Distribution", "Components", "Weights", "Mean (SD)"),
    Value = c(
      toupper(consensus$dist),
      length(consensus$components),
      paste(round(consensus$weights, 3), collapse = ", "),
      paste0(round(consensus$fit_summary$mean, 4), " (",
             round(consensus$fit_summary$sd, 4), ")")
    )
  ),
  caption = "Consensus prior from linear pooling of two experts."
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

Agreement between experts can be quantified by the Bhattacharyya
coefficient [@Bhattacharyya1943], which measures distributional overlap on
a scale from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical distributions). A coefficient
close to 1 supports pooling; a low coefficient indicates the experts'
beliefs are largely non-overlapping, in which case pooling may obscure
a genuine disagreement that should be reported separately.

## Prior-Data Conflict Diagnostics

Prior-data conflict occurs when the observed data is implausible under the
prior predictive distribution [@Box1980]. \CRANpkg{bayprior} computes four
complementary conflict metrics using a common Normal approximation to the
prior and to the observed-data likelihood (via their means and standard
errors), so that the same diagnostics apply uniformly whatever the prior's
distribution family or the data type:

- **Prior predictive p-value** [@Box1980]: the probability of observing
  data at least as extreme as the observed data under the prior predictive
  distribution.
- **Surprise index**: the standardised distance between the prior mean and
  the observed data, expressed in prior standard deviation units.
- **Information divergence**: the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the
  prior to the normalised likelihood.
- **Bhattacharyya overlap**: the distributional overlap between the prior
  and normalised likelihood.

```{r conflict}
interim <- list(type = "binary", x = 18, n = 40)
cd <- prior_conflict(prior, interim)
```

```{r cd-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Diagnostic = c("Box's p-value", "Surprise index", "KL divergence",
                    "Bhattacharyya overlap", "Conflict severity",
                    "Recommendation"),
    Value = c(
      round(cd$box_pvalue, 4),
      round(cd$surprise_index, 4),
      round(cd$kl_prior_likelihood, 4),
      round(cd$overlap, 4),
      toupper(cd$conflict_severity),
      cd$recommendation
    )
  ),
  caption = "Prior-data conflict diagnostics for the response rate prior.",
  booktabs = TRUE, linesep = ""
) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "3.5cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "9cm") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

Four data types are supported for the observed-data side of this
comparison: binary (event count out of a sample size), continuous
(observed mean and SD), Poisson/count (events over exposure), and survival
(events over total follow-up time); each is mapped internally to an
approximate mean and standard error before the Normal-approximation
diagnostics above are applied. This is distinct from the *exact* conjugate
posterior updates (Beta-Binomial, Normal-Normal, Gamma-Poisson,
Gamma-Exponential) that \CRANpkg{bayprior} uses elsewhere -- for example
in the sensitivity analysis module below -- to compute posterior summaries.

For co-primary endpoints, multivariate conflict can be assessed using the
Mahalanobis distance [@Mahalanobis1936]. The test assumes approximate
multivariate normality; for proportion endpoints such as the illustrative
example below, `bayprior`'s documentation recommends transforming to the
log-odds scale first. For simplicity, the example here uses raw
proportions directly:

```{r conflict-mv}
pm   <- c(0.35, 0.60)
pcov <- matrix(c(0.010, 0.003, 0.003, 0.015), 2, 2)
om   <- c(0.52, 0.58)
ocov <- matrix(c(2e-4, 4e-5, 4e-5, 2e-4), 2, 2)

mv <- conflict_mahalanobis(pm, pcov, om, ocov,
                           labels = c("Response rate", "OS rate"))
```

```{r mv-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Diagnostic = c("Mahalanobis D", "Chi-sq p-value (df=2)", "Conflict flag",
                    paste("z -", names(mv$marginal_z)), "Interpretation"),
    Value = c(
      round(mv$mahal_distance, 4),
      round(mv$pvalue, 4),
      as.character(mv$conflict_flag),
      round(mv$marginal_z, 3),
      mv$interpretation
    )
  ),
  caption = "Multivariate Mahalanobis conflict check for two co-primary endpoints.",
  booktabs = TRUE, linesep = ""
) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "3.5cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "9cm") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

## Sensitivity Analysis

The sensitivity module evaluates posterior conclusions across a
hyperparameter grid, answering the regulatory question: does the
treatment benefit conclusion change materially under plausible alternative
priors?

```{r sensitivity, fig.cap="Tornado plot showing the influence of prior hyperparameters on the posterior mean. Parameters are ranked by their marginal influence."}
sa <- sensitivity_grid(
  prior        = prior,
  data_summary = interim,
  param_grid   = list(
    alpha = seq(1, 8, by = 0.5),
    beta  = seq(2, 20, by = 1)
  ),
  target    = c("posterior_mean", "prob_efficacy"),
  threshold = 0.30
)
plot_tornado(sa)
```

The `sensitivity_cri()` function tracks credible interval width
specifically -- a quantity directly relevant to the precision of treatment
effect estimates in regulatory submissions.

## Robust, Sceptical, and Power Priors

\CRANpkg{bayprior} provides three alternative prior types for regulatory
sensitivity analyses.

**Robust mixture prior** [@Schmidli2014]: mixes the informative prior with
a vague component, protecting against prior misspecification:

```{r robust}
rob <- robust_prior(prior, vague_weight = 0.20)
plot(rob)
```

**Sceptical prior** [@Spiegelhalter1994]: centred at the null value of
the treatment effect, representing a conservative regulatory stance:

```{r sceptical}
scep <- sceptical_prior(
  null_value = 0.20,
  family     = "beta",
  strength   = "moderate",
  label      = "Response rate (sceptical)"
)
```

**Power prior** [@Ibrahim2000]: down-weights historical data by a factor
$\delta \in (0, 1]$ calibrated to achieve a target Bayes Factor:

```{r power-prior}
base  <- elicit_beta(mean = 0.50, sd = 0.20, method = "moments",
                     label = "Response rate")
calib <- calibrate_power_prior(
  historical_data = list(type = "binary", x = 12, n = 40),
  current_data    = list(type = "binary", x = 18, n = 50),
  base_prior      = base,
  target_bf       = 3
)
```

```{r calib-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Method", "Target BF", "Optimal delta",
                  "Power prior mean", "Power prior SD"),
    Value = c(
      calib$method,
      calib$target_bf,
      calib$delta_opt,
      round(calib$power_prior$fit_summary$mean, 4),
      round(calib$power_prior$fit_summary$sd, 4)
    )
  ),
  caption = "Power prior calibration via Bayes Factor."
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

## Regulatory Reporting

A single call to `prior_report()` generates a self-contained prior
justification document in HTML, PDF, or Word format:

```{r report, eval=FALSE}
prior_report(
  prior           = prior,
  conflict        = cd,
  sensitivity     = sa,
  robust_prior    = rob,
  sceptical_prior = scep,
  output_format   = "html",
  trial_name      = "TRIAL-001",
  sponsor         = "Example Pharma Ltd",
  author          = "N.P., Biostatistician"
)
```

The generated report includes parameter summary tables, all diagnostic
plots, a compliance checklist aligned with the FDA 2026 draft guidance
[@FDA2026], and a structured prior justification narrative.

# Case study: TRIAL-001

We demonstrate the complete \CRANpkg{bayprior} workflow on TRIAL-001, a
synthetic oncology Phase II trial with a binary response rate endpoint.
The target response rate is 30\% (null hypothesis) versus an expected
rate of 40\% (alternative hypothesis).

## Expert Elicitation and Pooling

Two clinical experts independently specified Beta priors for the response
rate. Expert 1 (conservative) placed a mean of 0.30 with SD of 0.08;
Expert 2 (optimistic) placed a mean of 0.42 with SD of 0.10. Equal weights
were assigned on the basis of comparable seniority.

```{r trial-elicitation}
e1 <- elicit_beta(mean = 0.30, sd = 0.08, method = "moments",
                  label = "Response rate", expert_id = "Expert_1")
e2 <- elicit_beta(mean = 0.42, sd = 0.10, method = "moments",
                  label = "Response rate", expert_id = "Expert_2")

pool <- aggregate_experts(list(E1 = e1, E2 = e2),
                          weights = c(0.5, 0.5),
                          method  = "linear")
```

```{r pool-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Quantity = c("Distribution", "Components", "Weights", "Mean (SD)"),
    Value = c(
      toupper(pool$dist),
      length(pool$components),
      paste(round(pool$weights, 3), collapse = ", "),
      paste0(round(pool$fit_summary$mean, 4), " (",
             round(pool$fit_summary$sd, 4), ")")
    )
  ),
  caption = "Consensus prior pooled from two clinical experts (TRIAL-001)."
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The two expert distributions overlap substantially (means 0.30 and
0.42 with comparable SDs of 0.08 and 0.10), supporting the use of
equal-weight linear pooling. The consensus prior had a mean of
`r round(pool$fit_summary$mean, 3)` and SD of
`r round(pool$fit_summary$sd, 3)`.

## Conflict Diagnostics at Interim

At the pre-specified interim analysis, 18 responses were observed in
40 patients (observed rate: 45\%).

```{r trial-conflict}
interim_data <- list(type = "binary", x = 18, n = 40)
cd_trial <- prior_conflict(pool, interim_data)
```

```{r cdtrial-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Diagnostic = c("Box's p-value", "Surprise index", "KL divergence",
                    "Bhattacharyya overlap", "Conflict severity",
                    "Recommendation"),
    Value = c(
      round(cd_trial$box_pvalue, 4),
      round(cd_trial$surprise_index, 4),
      round(cd_trial$kl_prior_likelihood, 4),
      round(cd_trial$overlap, 4),
      toupper(cd_trial$conflict_severity),
      cd_trial$recommendation
    )
  ),
  caption = "Prior-data conflict diagnostics at the TRIAL-001 interim analysis.",
  booktabs = TRUE, linesep = ""
) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "3.5cm") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "9cm") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The Box p-value was above the 0.10 threshold, indicating no evidence of
prior-data conflict. The posterior distribution updated the consensus prior
towards the observed data as expected.

## Regulatory Sensitivity Pair

Following FDA guidance recommendations, we computed an enthusiastic-sceptical
prior sensitivity pair:

```{r trial-sensitivity-pair}
scep_trial <- sceptical_prior(null_value = 0.20, family = "beta",
                              strength = "moderate",
                              label = "Response rate (sceptical)")

cd_scep <- prior_conflict(scep_trial, interim_data)

cat("Conflict severity (consensus): ",
    cd_trial$conflict_severity, "\n")
cat("Conflict severity (sceptical):",
    cd_scep$conflict_severity, "\n")
```

Conclusions were consistent across both priors, supporting regulatory
robustness.

# Discussion

\CRANpkg{bayprior} provides a structured workflow for prior justification
that addresses a practical gap in the Bayesian clinical trial toolkit. The
package is designed to be used alongside existing analysis packages
(\CRANpkg{RBesT}, \CRANpkg{rstanarm}, \CRANpkg{brms}) rather than
replacing them: bayprior handles the prior specification phase, and
established packages handle the posterior computation.

## Regulatory Alignment

The FDA's 2026 draft guidance on Bayesian methods [@FDA2026] asks sponsors
relying on a Bayesian analysis to provide detailed support for the
proposed prior distribution and any external information borrowing, to
quantify the prior's influence (for example via an effective sample
size), to evaluate operating characteristics -- including sensitivity to
the prior specification and to prior-data conflict, typically via
simulation -- and to document the analysis in sufficient detail for the
FDA to understand and, where feasible, reproduce it. \CRANpkg{bayprior}
supports each of these expectations directly: structured elicitation and
pooling provide a documented, reproducible derivation of the prior; the
sensitivity, robust, sceptical, and power prior modules provide alternative
specifications for demonstrating robustness; and the regulatory reporting
module assembles this into a single submission-ready document.

Prior-data conflict and the influence of external information are also a
recurring theme in EMA guidance on incorporating historical or external
data. The EMA reflection paper on extrapolation in paediatric drug
development [@EMA2018], for instance, requires sponsors to quantify how
much information a Bayesian prior contributes relative to the data
generated in the target population and to investigate the Type I error
properties of the resulting analysis. The conflict diagnostics in
\CRANpkg{bayprior} -- the Box predictive p-value, surprise index,
information divergence, and Bhattacharyya overlap -- provide a closed-form
way to address this for conjugate prior families, without requiring a
fitted model.

## Shiny Application

The bundled Shiny application mirrors the package's six modules as
separate panels, allowing a biostatistician without R programming
experience to perform the same elicitation, pooling, conflict, sensitivity,
robust prior, and reporting workflow interactively. Each panel produces the
same plots and summary statistics as the corresponding R function, and the
final regulatory report can be downloaded directly from the application.
The application is hosted at
<https://ndohpenn-bayprior.share.connect.posit.cloud> and can be launched
locally via `run_app()`.

## Limitations

Several limitations apply to the current release (v0.3.0). The
multivariate Mahalanobis check is currently limited to bivariate (k = 2)
endpoints; extension to k $\geq$ 3 co-primary endpoints is planned for a
future release. Survival power priors require numerical integration over
the partial likelihood and are not yet implemented; calibrated power priors
are currently available for binary, continuous, Poisson, and log-normal
data types. The robust mixture prior uses a Normal vague component
regardless of the informative prior family; for Beta, Gamma, and other
non-Normal informative priors, the resulting mixture density is computed
numerically rather than analytically, which is accurate in the body of the
distribution but may be less reliable in the extreme tails.

Future development includes survival power priors, k $\geq$ 3 endpoint
Mahalanobis conflict, and interoperability with \CRANpkg{RBesT} for MAP
prior workflows. A companion paper in Pharmaceutical Statistics
(in preparation) provides a methodological treatment of the conflict
diagnostic framework and a regulatory alignment assessment against the
FDA 2026 draft guidance and ICH E9(R1).

# Summary

\CRANpkg{bayprior} provides an integrated R tool for the complete prior
justification workflow in Bayesian clinical trials, combining structured
expert elicitation, opinion pooling, conjugate conflict diagnostics,
hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, robust prior alternatives, and
regulatory reporting in a single package. The package is available on CRAN:

```{r install-cran, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("bayprior")
```

The full documentation and vignettes are available at
<https://ndohpenngit.github.io/bayprior/>. A live Shiny application
is hosted at <https://ndohpenn-bayprior.share.connect.posit.cloud>.

```{r citation, echo=FALSE}
cat(format(citation("bayprior"), style = "text"), sep = "\n")
```
